title: Intentions in prayer
hookLine: mystical meditations attached to the words of prayer

lines: AN HOUR BEFORE THE FIRST WORD.
cards: The Mishnah remembers a group it calls the pious ones of old. Before they prayed, it says, they would wait an hour, just to direct their hearts toward God. A whole hour of getting ready, before the first word.
Some mornings, finding the right page is as far as anyone gets. But the question they were answering is an old and practical one. When the mouth says the words, where is the heart pointed?
Later kabbalists answered it in fine detail.

teach.b: Kavanot. The plural of kavanah: intention, the direction of the heart. First, the old rule.
The Mishnah imagines someone reading the Torah aloud who reaches the passage of the Shema just as the time comes to say it. Does it count as their Shema?
If they directed their heart, the Mishnah says, they have fulfilled it. Intention is what turns reading into prayer. Second, the kabbalists' kavanot.

Luria and his students taught particular meditations to hold while saying the words of the prayers: divine names, the sefirot, the joining of one to another. A single word in the prayer book could carry a whole map.
Some prayer books print these meditations beside the words, for those who pray with them. Third, a short doorway.

Before doing a commandment, some Jews say a line that begins l'shem yichud, for the sake of the unification, naming the Holy One and the Shechinah, the indwelling presence from earlier in this stretch.
In the kabbalists' language, the act joins what had been apart. Fourth, the Hasidic turn.

teach.h: THE SIMPLER WAY: THE WHOLE HEART.
teach.b: Some Hasidic teachers taught a simpler kavanah for people who would never learn the full meditations: pray with your whole heart, cling to the words, let them carry you. Every one of these keeps the words the same.
What changes is where the heart is pointed. Two people can say the same blessing over the same bread. One is reciting it.

how: Kavanah, directing the heart, is taught as part of Jewish prayer; in kabbalistic circles, some pray from prayer books that print Lurianic meditations beside the words, and some say a line beginning l'shem yichud before a commandment.

o: the melodies used to chant the Torah aloud
the fixed times of day set for each prayer
intentions held in the heart while saying prayers

games.q: the heart's direction — tap the pairs.

s: in the Mishnah, intention can decide whether the Shema counts
if the reader directed their heart, the Mishnah says, they fulfilled it.
the kavanot are new prayers added to the service
they are meditations held while saying the same words.
the Mishnah's pious ones began praying the moment they arrived
they waited an hour, to direct their hearts toward God.

games.q: you're reading the Torah aloud and reach the Shema passage just as its time arrives. by the Mishnah, does it count as your Shema?
o: yes, always, once the words are said.
only if you directed your heart.
never: you have to start again.
games.why: the Mishnah says it counts if the reader directed their heart: intention turns reading into prayer.

practice: If you say blessings, choose one you know well, over bread, over water, on waking; if you don't, choose a simple thank-you you say often.
Before the words, pause and ask what exactly you're pointing them toward: this glass of water, the person who cooked, the body that's thirsty, God, if you pray.
Then say the words slowly, with that one intention riding on them, and rest in the quiet after.

wordCard.voice: Kavanot. Intentions: meditations attached to the words of prayer, so the heart is pointed somewhere while the mouth speaks. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: intentions; the singular, kavanah, is the direction of the heart.

carryVoice: Your line: intend. The same words can be recited by the mouth, or meant by the heart. Rest well.
